kurz: Three fund structures track the same index and differ in risks, costs and taxation.

bloecke.md: An index is a set of rules and not yet a portfolio. To turn the instruction “weight around 1,250 shares by free-float market capitalisation” into a tradable fund unit, the provider has to decide how the fund is built. This decision is not apparent from the product name. There are three usual approaches: buying the entire index, approximating it with a selection of its constituents, or having a bank deliver its return. Funds built in these ways have almost identical price paths. They differ in transaction costs, in the kind of risk the investor bears and in taxation, which has particularly large consequences in Germany.

## Full replication

In full physical replication, the fund holds every index constituent at its weight in the index. The iShares Core S&P 500 (IE00B5BMR087) holds 503 positions for an index of 500 companies. The difference is due to multiple listings such as the two Alphabet share classes. With fund assets of around €133.9 billion as of 31 July 2026, it is the largest ETF launched in Europe, and its TER is 0.07%.

The drawback of this exact replication is the large number of transactions. Index changes, corporate actions, dividends and inflows each trigger real orders, and every order costs the spread and a fee. As long as the index consists of 500 highly liquid large companies, this hardly matters. If the index also contains many small stocks, full replication becomes expensive. These trading costs are not included in the TER; they reduce the fund's value directly.

## Optimised sampling

The FTSE All-World contains around 4,200 stocks from 49 countries, including many small stocks in markets with low liquidity. The Vanguard FTSE All-World (IE00BK5BQT80, 0.14% TER) holds 3,759 positions. Around 450 index members are therefore not included in the fund.

In optimised sampling, an optimiser deliberately selects the subset so that the risk structure of the index (country weights, sectors, size classes, currencies, factor profile) is matched as closely as possible. It leaves out stocks that cause high trading costs and contribute little to replicating the index. In return, an additional replication error arises, which is barely noticeable in calm markets and becomes visible during index changes or periods of stress. It can work in either direction, so the fund can fall short of the index or beat it by a few basis points.

The stated replication method can be misleading here. The iShares Core MSCI World (IE00B4L5Y983) is officially classified as a sampling fund, yet with around 1,250 positions it holds practically the entire index. The number of positions relative to the breadth of the index is therefore more informative than the information in the factsheet.

bloecke.titel: Index breadth and number of positions held
bloecke.unter: For the S&P 500 and the MSCI World, sampling hardly plays a role; in the FTSE All-World fund, around 450 stocks are missing.

bloecke.md:
## Synthetic replication via swaps

A synthetically replicating ETF does not buy the shares in the index. It holds a substitute basket of liquid shares, mostly European and Japanese blue chips, which need not have anything to do with the target index. The fund enters into a total return swap with a bank. Under this swap, the fund delivers the return of its substitute basket and the bank delivers the return of the index. This *unfunded* variant is the norm today. In the *funded* variant, the fund transfers money to the counterparty and in return has collateral placed in a pledged account.

As a result, the fund tracks the index very closely, because the index return is agreed by contract and does not first have to be achieved through purchases and sales. Swaps are therefore used where buying the index physically is laborious or impossible, for example for commodity indices, individual emerging markets and very broad indices. Providers also use them for standard US indices because of US withholding tax. The Invesco S&P 500 (IE00B3YCGJ38) uses unfunded swaps and has a TER of 0.05%. With fund assets of around €49.6 billion, it is Europe's fifth-largest ETF. The Amundi Core S&P 500 Swap, at €29.8 billion, is also among the ten largest. Synthetic replication is therefore a large market segment.

bloecke.formel: Fund assets = Substitute basket + Swap value
bloecke.erklaerung: The swap value is the difference, accumulated since the last settlement, between the index return and the return of the substitute basket. It can be positive or negative. The counterparty owes the fund something only when it is positive, and only this amount constitutes the open counterparty risk.
variablen: Basket of liquid shares that the fund actually owns and that belongs to the segregated fund assets
Claim on or liability to the counterparty, revalued daily
bloecke.beispiel: Index +3.0% since the last settlement, substitute basket +2.4%: the swap value is +0.6% of fund assets in the fund's favour. This 0.6% is what would be at stake if the counterparty became insolvent, calculated before taking the collateral into account.

bloecke.unter: The substitute basket remains the property of the fund; only the outstanding difference in returns is settled via the swap.

bloecke.md:
## Size of the counterparty risk

The UCITS rules limit the value of all derivative positions with a single counterparty to 10% of net asset value if the counterparty is a credit institution, and to 5% otherwise (Article 52 of the UCITS Directive). For German funds, this limit is laid down in Section 27 DerivateV (Derivatives Ordinance); for ETFs launched in Ireland, it is laid down in the identically worded Irish implementation. In practice, the open swap value is far below this. It is regularly reset to zero by a settlement payment, usually daily or as soon as it exceeds a threshold. In addition, there is collateral, with usual coverage ratios of 100% to 120% of the swap value and up to around 130% for funded swaps. Large providers also spread the swap across several banks. For the Invesco S&P 500 there are five, including Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley and Nomura.

If a counterparty defaults, the investor therefore does not lose their capital, because the substitute basket still belongs to the fund. What is at risk is the open swap value, and this is collateralised. A realisation and valuation risk remains, because the collateral then has to be sold in a disrupted market in which its prices are also under pressure.

Physical ETFs also carry counterparty risk, through securities lending. The fund lends shares to market participants who need them for short selling and receives a fee in return. The lent securities are typically overcollateralised at 102% to 105% and valued daily at market prices. At iShares, 62.5% of lending income goes into the fund assets and the provider keeps 37.5%.

The iShares Core MSCI World shows that this income matters. With a TER of 0.20%, its average deviation from the index since 2010 has been only around 0.03 percentage points a year. A considerable part of the management fee is therefore recouped through lending and the treatment of withholding tax. Investors who want to avoid securities lending have to look in the annual report, because the product name and the word “physical” give no information about it.

## US withholding tax as a reason for swaps

The US generally levies 30% withholding tax on dividends from American companies. A fund launched in Ireland pays only 15% thanks to the 1997 double taxation agreement, while a Luxembourg physical fund in practice pays the full 30%. The indices that are qualified under US law include the S&P 500 and the MSCI World. Under certain conditions, a swap on such an index does not trigger withholding tax on the dividend component (IRC Section 871(m)), because the fund does not own the US shares.

Since the 2018 investment tax reform, German private investors can no longer credit foreign withholding tax against their own tax. This leakage does not appear on any tax document; it reduces the fund's value directly.

bloecke.unter: With the same index and the same shares, three different tax rates apply at fund level, depending on the fund structure.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation of withholding tax leakage over 30 years

bloecke.md: The calculation assumes an S&P 500 ETF with an index return of 7.00% before withholding tax and a US dividend yield of 1.6%. This corresponds to the average of the S&P 500 dividend yields at the year-ends from 2016 to 2025. In October 2026, the yield was around 1.0%, so the leakage was smaller (around 0.16 percentage points at 15% withholding tax). TER, trading costs and German tax are left out, since the only point is the order of magnitude of the withholding tax effect. For a world ETF, the advantage is smaller, because only around 73% of the MSCI World is in US shares. With the same assumptions, the leakage there with an Irish domicile is around 0.18 percentage points (73% of 0.24). According to analyses by justETF, the measured return advantage of synthetic S&P 500 ETFs over physical ones is around 0.12 to 0.26 percentage points a year. This confirms the illustrative calculation approximately but not exactly, and higher total costs can offset the advantage again.

## Partial exemption in Germany

German investors receive a partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% on income from equity funds (Section 20 InvStG, Investment Tax Act). It compensates on a flat-rate basis for the fact that the fund already pays 15% corporation tax on domestic dividends. The decisive factor is the investment conditions (Anlagebedingungen) rather than the securities the fund currently holds. The investment conditions must contain a binding commitment that more than 50% is continuously invested in equity participations (Section 2(6) InvStG).

This is where synthetic structures can fail the requirement. An ETF whose substitute basket economically delivers 100% of the index return receives a 0% partial exemption if it does not commit to an equity ratio in its prospectus. The large providers adjusted their investment conditions after 2018. Today, the problem therefore affects only individual swap and specialised products.

bloecke.titel: Advantage of 0.24 percentage points, disadvantage of €791
bloecke.md:
A portfolio is worth €30,000, of which €10,000 is price gain. It is sold after ten years. The flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) is 25% plus solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total, and the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) has already been used up.

- With a 30% partial exemption, 10,000 × 0.70 = €7,000 is taxable. 26.375% of this gives €1,846.25 in tax.
- Without partial exemption, €10,000 is taxable. 26.375% of this gives €2,637.50 in tax.
- The difference is €791.25.

The withholding tax advantage of 0.24 percentage points brings around €72 a year for a portfolio of this size. Calculated with these fixed amounts, the loss of the partial exemption would be offset after around eleven years. The disadvantage grows too, however, because the price gain that is taxed without the partial exemption grows along with the portfolio, and because the extra return of the swap fund is also taxed in full. For a lump-sum investment with the returns from the illustrative calculation (6.76% physical, 7.00% via swap) and tax only on sale, the swap fund comes out ahead after tax only after around 43 years. The advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale), which is taxed more heavily every year without partial exemption, pushes this point even further out. The tax classification of the fund therefore has a greater effect than the replication mechanism itself.

punkte: The fund owns the index shares itself, and the structure can be understood without knowledge of the contracts
The partial exemption is practically always assured for the large products
The provider exercises the voting rights, which is relevant for investors interested in corporate governance
No swap partner whose creditworthiness also has to be assessed
Closer tracking of the index, because the replication is owed under the contract
For US indices, 0% instead of 15% or 30% withholding tax
Access to markets and commodities that can hardly be replicated physically
On the other hand, there is counterparty risk and dependence on a US tax rule that can be changed

bloecke.md: The tax classification is checked first, that is, whether the prospectus commits to more than 50% equity participations. This is followed by the fund domicile, the replication method and the number of positions held relative to the breadth of the index. In this order, the influence on the final result decreases.

bloecke.titel: Where to find the information in the fund documents
bloecke.md:
- The factsheet shows the replication method, the number of positions and the domicile, which can be recognised from the ISIN (IE = Ireland, LU = Luxembourg).
- The key information document (PRIIPs KID) contains the risk warnings and the reference to the use of derivatives.
- In the prospectus, the section on the investment conditions contains the binding equity ratio commitment that decides the partial exemption. If it is missing, the 30% is lost.
- The annual report lists the swap counterparties, the collateral ratio, and the scope and income of securities lending, that is, information that the fund name does not give.

bloecke.titel: Swap variants in the event of insolvency
bloecke.md:
With an **unfunded swap**, the investors' money remains in the substitute basket, which the fund owns itself. The swap claim covers only the accumulated difference in returns. If the bank defaults, the fund still owns a share portfolio and merely has to replicate the difference to the index or write it off.

With a **funded swap**, the fund transfers the money to the counterparty and receives collateral in return, which is placed in a pledged account with a third-party depositary. Coverage is therefore higher, often around 130%. If the counterparty defaults, everything depends on the pledge being effective and on the collateral being realisable. This structure is the exception among European UCITS ETFs today.

For a broad global portfolio, the replication method is rarely the most important criterion. Large physical funds on the MSCI World or FTSE All-World have tracked their index reliably for years, and the withholding tax advantage of a swap is considerably smaller for an index with a 27% non-US share than for the S&P 500. The question becomes important for a pure US building block, where the effect is greatest, and for niche indices where buying the constituents physically is expensive or impossible. In both cases, what matters is the result after German tax and after costs, and the fund structure determines it only in part.

mitnehmen: Full replication, sampling and swaps track the same index but bring different risks that are not apparent from the product name.

The counterparty risk of a swap is limited to 10% of fund assets per counterparty (Article 52 of the UCITS Directive), is reset continuously and is collateralised at 100% to 120%, so a total loss due to the structure is ruled out.

Physical ETFs are not automatically less risky, because securities lending also creates counterparty risk; at the same time, the income from lending explains why some ETFs track their index almost free of cost.

The swap structure brings a measurable return advantage mainly for US shares, because 0% instead of 15% or 30% withholding tax is due there; measured, this comes to around 0.12 to 0.26 percentage points a year.
If the investment conditions lack the ratio commitment, the 30% partial exemption is lost (Section 2(6), Section 20 InvStG), and this disadvantage usually outweighs any withholding tax advantage.

begriffe.text: Physical replication with a subset of the index constituents. An optimiser selects the positions so that the country, sector and size structure of the index is matched, and leaves out illiquid micro-caps. This saves trading costs and creates a small additional replication error.

Instead of the index shares, the fund holds a substitute basket and swaps its return for the index return via a total return swap. This results in very close tracking of the index, combined with counterparty risk.

The basket of liquid securities that a synthetically replicating ETF owns itself. It belongs to the fund assets, which are kept separate from the assets of the management company, and its content need not have anything to do with the target index.

The risk that a contractual partner fails to meet its obligation. For swap-based ETFs, it is limited to 10% of fund assets per credit institution (Article 52 of the UCITS Directive), is reset continuously and is typically collateralised at 100% to 120%.

The fund lends shares in return for a fee and collateral, usually with 102% to 105% overcollateralisation and daily valuation. Lending improves the result relative to the index but also creates counterparty risk for physical ETFs.
